This retrospective case study asks how partially preserved historical machine-learning research can be reconstructed while distinguishing source-equivalent computation, compatibility with archived outputs, measurement authority, public reproducibility, and predictive validity.
The archive supports eight historical scientific formulations and nine neural model families.
Public records identify their structures; original route qualification remains a privately recorded result.
Those records report exact equality between the recovered reference implementation and original central processing unit (CPU) outputs for all 18 routes.
Comparisons with archived graphics processing unit (GPU) arrays pass for M0--M3 and fail for both repeats of M4--M8 under the unchanged tolerance.

Mean six-cell normalized root-mean-square error (NRMSE) was 2.430659 for zero innovation, 1.036038 for the training-mean baseline, 0.736270 for ridge regression, and 0.773316 for the structured comparator.
These descriptive synthetic results do not estimate predictive performance of the historical model families.

Goodman and colleagues describe reproducibility terminology as unsettled across fields; we therefore report the operation and evidence for each result instead of assigning one binary label \cite{R15}.

The NeurIPS reproducibility program described by Pineau and colleagues combined code policy, a community challenge, and a submission checklist to improve prospective reporting and evaluation \cite{R9}.
The present work applies those concerns retrospectively to one archive and does not claim that checklists or existing research infrastructure are absent \cite{R1}.

MLflow Tracking documents APIs for recording parameters, code versions, metrics, and output artifacts for runs; DVC documents experiment management alongside data, model, and pipeline versioning \cite{R19,R20}.

Provenance and research-object standards address related needs: W3C PROV-O supplies a vocabulary for provenance entities and activities, while RO-Crate specifies packaging of research objects and their metadata \cite{R17,R18}.
FAIR4RS describes findability, accessibility, interoperability, and reusability goals for research software \cite{R7}.
Force-time outcomes depend on event boundaries and measurement procedures; they do not make force and impulse interchangeable outcomes \cite{R3,R4}.

The case study distinguishes eight historical scientific formulations from nine original neural model families, identified in the source archive as M0--M8 and each represented by two repeats (r0 and r1).

ACM's Artifact Review and Badging policy v1.1 separates artifact evaluation, public artifact availability, and results validation; functional and reusable artifacts are distinct evaluation levels \cite{R16}.
Floating-point literature shows why numerical comparison must be tied to a stated operation and tolerance; it does not identify the cause of the discrepancies in this archive \cite{R2,R13}.
CMJ reporting literature emphasizes that selected force-time metrics and their measurement procedures should be explicit \cite{R3,R4}.
TRIPOD-Cluster motivates transparent descriptions of clustered development and validation data \cite{R5}, but its reporting guidance does not make synthetic camps equivalent to human cohorts.
Morris, White, and Crowther propose the ADEMP structure—Aims, Data-generating mechanisms, Estimands, Methods, and Performance measures—for planning and reporting simulation studies \cite{R12}.
